title: Unlocking Data To Identify Wealth Management Prospects in Bank Branches
summary: How banks can leverage data to size the wealth advisor opportunity by branch, align incentives, and find affluent customers.
body_markdown:
The concept of banks offering investment services in their branches isn’t new. Banks in the U.S. sold stocks and bonds directly to consumers until the Great Depression exposed risky and unethical behavior. In 1933, Congress passed the Glass-Steagall Act, which meant an investment bank and a commercial bank could no longer sit under the same holding company. For example, J.P. Morgan & Co. chose commercial banking, and as a result, partners Henry S. Morgan and Harold Stanley left to form Morgan Stanley.1


Deregulation in the 1990s blurred the line between commercial and investment banking. Today, Fed regulations still prohibit FDIC-insured bank employees from providing brokerage activities. However, bank holding companies can own brokerage firms, and employees of those brokerage subsidiaries can give investment advice to clients at branch locations. The question is: how do you effectively identify those potential clients?


## Opportunity assessment


A quick way to spot wealth management opportunities among customers or prospects is to assign each one to an Affluence Segment. These segments are a useful shortcut for understanding a client’s investment product needs, and how much personal advice they need and are willing to pay for. Segments are generally assigned based on a household’s estimated total financial assets:


- Ultra high net worth ($10 million+)
- High net worth ($1-10 million)
- Mass affluent ($0.5-$1 million)
- Emerging mass affluent (households on an income path to becoming “mass affluent” soon)2


An advisor’s sales opportunity in a branch can be identified by how many of the branch’s customers fall into the Affluent Segments. Third-party demographic data can help size the number of prospects in each segment within the branch’s primary trade area.


But investment advisory is a very competitive business. Banks compete with stand-alone brokerage firms like Charles Schwab and Edward Jones, as well as self-directed providers like Vanguard and Fidelity Investments. To build credibility and stand out, advisors at traditional bank holding companies often lean on legacy brokerage brands the bank owns, such as Merrill Lynch, which Bank of America acquired in 2008.


## The advisor vs branch manager conflict


To build a book of business, a wealth management advisor in a branch depends heavily on referrals from the branch manager. At many banks, the branch manager is paid directly for making those referrals.


However, banks need to manage the potential for conflict between those two roles if they work in the same branch. Growth in traditional branch products, such as time deposits, can suffer when advisors promote mutual funds to the branch’s best customers. A less visible but often more pressing conflict arises when an advisor promotes a credit product secured by investment balances, which competes directly with traditional lending products such as unsecured personal loans and home equity loans.


Banks with captive investment advisors need to think carefully about keeping the branch manager and the advisor aligned, especially since the advisor serves many of the branch’s best deposit customers. One approach is a joint compensation plan that rewards both the advisor and the branch manager based on the client’s total funds with the bank holding company, combining deposit balances and assets under management in investment accounts.


## How Teradata can help


Assigning customers and prospects to an Affluence Segment is critical to sizing the wealth management opportunity at the branch level. Doing it well takes sophisticated models that pick up subtle patterns in payments data showing cross-shopping with investment advisors, as well as cash flow patterns that let you infer annual income based on similar customers.


Teradata’s “Payments 360” Data Product speeds up the process of pulling out these insights. Unstructured data, such as inbound call transcripts, can also reveal customer financial needs that are hard to see in structured data alone. Teradata’s[Customer Journey Analytics](https://www.teradata.com/resources/white-papers/customer-journey-analytics-in-banking) data product provides the infrastructure to analyze call transcripts and email messages.
